https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/gov.text: The Budapest Times Government sinks barges in Danube to protect nuclear plant output The controlled sinking of the barges has begun, and water levels at the pumping station have already risen by one centimetre, while a continuous drop in water levels continues to be recorded in the main channel of the Danube — the Prime Minister announced on Saturday morning in Paks, at a press conference held beside the nuclear power plant's cold-water canal. Péter Magyar stressed that without intervention, water levels in the Danube would fall so low by Sunday night that one of the two still-operating turbines would have to be shut down, with a complete shutdown to follow later. The sinking of the barges and the construction of a sill are intended to prevent this, he said. “Our goal is to maintain the operation of the two functioning turbines and, through the construction of the sill, to raise the Danube’s water level sufficiently so that the turbines can be brought back online gradually and safely,” the Prime Minister stated. The Prime Minister outlined that the cabinet decided on Wednesday to launch the Paks investment aimed at raising the Danube’s water level, based on the plans received, the projected water level data, and the known meteorological forecasts. The work consists of two parts: the construction of a sill, for which 145,000 cubic metres of rock will be used, and the positioning, securing, rotation, and controlled sinking of two barges, each 80 metres long, placed side by side. Péter Magyar said the water level in the area was around minus 120–122 centimetres. According to forecasts, on Sunday night or Monday morning the water level in the main channel of the Danube could drop to minus 132 centimetres, at which point one of the two still-operational turbines would have to be shut down. Based on water management forecasts, the water level could fall to as low as minus 140 centimetres within five to six days, which would necessitate a complete shutdown of the nuclear power plant, he said. “We must prevent this from happening, and we will prevent it,” he declared. He recalled that just a few weeks earlier, the Paks nuclear power plant had come within millimetres of having to be shut down. The plant’s eight turbines are capable of a combined output of 2,000 megawatts, but currently only two turbines are operating, generating approximately 500 megawatts, he explained. A prolonged shutdown of Paks would be a “massive blow” to the Hungarian economy, businesses, the population, and the national budget alike, he added. Experts examined several possible solutions. Among those considered were blocking the nuclear power plant’s cooling water intake channel with wing walls or stones, as well as raising the water level using pumping stations, Péter Magyar reported. The Hungarian Atomic Energy Authority and the relevant authorities considered these to be poor solutions from a nuclear safety standpoint, he said. He stressed that “maintaining our country’s nuclear safety is the single most important priority,” and for this reason those proposals were rejected, and the decision was made together with the experts to construct a sill weir instead. The last similar operation was carried out in 1995, near Dunakiliti, though under easier conditions, with more time for planning and construction, the Prime Minister recalled. He said “the Danube has now given us only a few days.” The work is progressing well, according to plan, and at an increasingly rapid pace, he reported. Around five thousand tonnes of rock will arrive in Paks and Dunaszentbenedek throughout the day, and work is proceeding simultaneously on both banks of the Danube, he added. According to Péter Magyar’s account, the two barges arrived from Mohács, and water management specialists have been working for two days on the necessary dredging, securing, and positioning. On Saturday morning, their controlled, monitored, and supervised submersion began — initially by around 20 centimetres. The Prime Minister called the investment a national matter, one which he said requires full national unity. Hundreds of soldiers, police officers, water management specialists, contractors, industrial divers, engineers, and planners are working together on the project, he stressed. Péter Magyar described it as regrettable and telling that neither the former prime minister nor the leaders of other parliamentary parties had accepted his invitation to view the investment securing the power plant’s operation. He stated that, to their knowledge, all of them are holidaying abroad at this time. He added that “they did not offer help of their own accord (…), they did not call for full national unity (…) they flooded the internet with disinformation and lies” and tried to mislead their fellow citizens. Péter Magyar also spoke about what questions he would have asked Viktor Orbán, the president of Fidesz, had he gone to Paks. Among other things, he said he would have asked why the upgrade to the Paks water intake and pumping system — recommended by experts following the record-low water levels in 2018 — had never been carried out, an upgrade which, he said, would have cost 10 billion forints and ensured the full operational capacity of the Paks nuclear power plant even at water levels on the Danube lower than those currently being experienced. He would also have asked the prime minister why the possibility of constructing a sill had not been examined and prepared earlier, and “why and how Hungary ended up, after 16 years of governance, in a situation where the sinking of two 80-metre barges and the preparation of contingency plans are needed to maintain the operational capacity of Paks.” He would further have expected an answer as to why no strategic reserve water intake system had been developed that would be capable of serving all four Paks units even during a historic drought. He would also have asked the prime minister why Hungary’s energy system had not been prepared for the possibility that Paks output could temporarily drop significantly, and why sufficient energy storage capacity had not been built up. Finally, he said he would have asked Viktor Orbán whether he truly considers Hungary’s energy security a matter of national importance — and if so, why he did not go to Paks. Brigadier General Pál Kádár, head of the Defence Administration Office, reported at the press conference that after the initial capacities had been established, the investment to raise the water level of the Danube was proceeding on schedule by Saturday, though there is a shortage of stone-carrying trucks. He said that at any given time, 80 to 100 trucks are operating on both banks of the Danube between the quarries and the storage sites; these are two- and three-axle, steel-platform articulated vehicles. Work is carried out 24 hours a day. Pál Kádár expressed his thanks to all those supporting the investment with offers of assistance, and said that by late Friday evening 112 such offers had been received, a number that has since grown to 176. Answering questions, Péter Magyar stated that it would be irresponsible to name a precise date for when another turbine could be brought back online, or when the Paks nuclear power plant could resume full-capacity operation. According to the schedule, 30 days are available to install the 35,000 cubic metres of stone needed for the sill, followed by a further month in which 110,000 cubic metres of stone must be installed to preserve the stability of the waterworks. After that, the plant’s management can consider gradually reconnecting the turbines. In addition, the scheduled maintenance of one of the units is currently under way and must be completed before reconnection. The prime minister emphasized that the first task is maintaining nuclear safety. The second is avoiding a complete shutdown of Paks — that is, ensuring the continued operation of the two turbines currently running — followed by reconnecting as many turbines as possible. This requires increasingly rapid coordinated construction and flood defence simultaneously. Responding to a question about the risks of sinking the barges, Péter Magyar explained that the barges had been stabilized with two five-tonne anchors. In addition, the vessels were secured with thick steel cables to piles drilled eight metres deep and to concrete pillars. Everything had been doubly over-secured. Should they shift nonetheless, tugboats capable of stabilizing and repositioning the barges are standing by, he added. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjdv.text: Figure caption, Mamdani, Jon Stewart reveal new 9/11 documents By Madeline Halpert and Kayla Epstein Reporting from New York Published 8 September 2026, 14:27 BST Updated 2 hours ago Toxic air quality was being recorded in Manhattan soon after the 9/11 attacks even as officials played down health risks to the public, according to a trove of newly released files. Asbestos was found "nearly everywhere" tested near Ground Zero, where the World Trade Center towers collapsed in 2001, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air," he said, announcing the release of 170,000 documents related to the attacks. Illnesses related to the dust and smoke from the towers' collapse have claimed more lives than the nearly 3,000 who died in the attacks, US health officials say. Figure caption, BBC speaks with those affected by toxic air at Ground Zero Thousands of people have experienced health effects like cancer, including many who have died, after breathing in hazardous contaminants after the Twin Towers collapsed. Speaking alongside Mamdani at Tuesday's news conference, TV host and 9/11 survivor advocate Jon Stewart said the new files show the city knew by October 2001 - a month after the terrorist attacks - that the air in Manhattan was toxic. "So to be fair to them, they only buried that information for 25 years," he said sarcastically. The records show asbestos was found near Ground Zero for months after the attacks at the same time people were being advised it was safe to go there. The files, which include air-quality reports and communications among city officials, include October 2001 correspondence known as the "Harding Memo". In it, an aide warned former Deputy Mayor Robert Harding that the city could face as many as 35,000 legal claims for its response to the attacks. The document states that the city could be sued because health advisories caused individuals "to return to the area too soon (causing toxic exposure or emotional harm)". City officials also told citizens to clean up dust and debris with "wet mops and rags" despite the presence of asbestos, which is only supposed to be cleaned by licensed professionals, according to another memo documenting the concerns of congressman Jerry Nadler. Image source, Corey Sipkin/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images The memo pointed to testimony from the city's top health official at the time saying a study had found "no elevated levels of asbestos in indoor air", but that tests showed dust had "low levels of asbestos in some samples". The memo, attributed to Ester Fuchs, a special adviser at the time to Mayor Michael Bloomberg, acknowledged "potential problems for City Hall". Days after the attack, city and federal officials - including the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) - declared that the air near the Twin Towers was safe. Christine Todd Whitman, the head of the EPA at the time, later apologised for this declaration, saying the agency "did the very best we could at the time with the knowledge we had". Image source, Anthony Correia / Getty Images Firefighter describes emotional 9/11 stair climb Published 2 days ago Toxic dust legacy of 9/11 plagues thousands of people Published 1 September 2011 Tuesday's release of documents resolves a lawsuit brought by advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch, which sued after officials said they did not have the records. City officials found 68 boxes of documents last year. The pages of air quality reports and other records were released through an online portal timed for this Friday's 25th anniversary of the attacks. More documents are to be shared over the next year. Karen Klingon, who was involved in the 9/11 Health Watch lawsuit, told the BBC on Tuesday her brother lived five minutes away from Ground Zero. He developed asthma, was later diagnosed with cancer and died at 61 of a related brain tumor. Image source, Courtsey of Andrea Axelrod Image caption, Robert Klingon, who lived near the World Trader Center on September 11 and died of cancer in 2020. "There's a lot of research, probably, that can be done about what was in the air, and the kind of illnesses that derived of those toxins that were in the air, like what happened to my brother," she said. "Hopefully it helps people that were sick know and in the future." Phil Alvarez, whose brother Luis Alvarez died of cancer in 2019 after exposure to Ground Zero toxins, told the BBC that people "continue to get sick every single day, continue to die". https://www.dw.com/en/japan-us-marine-ar.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NjCd The US Marine Corps confirmed that a serviceman based at Marine Corps Air Station at Futenma, Okinawa, was in Japanese custody Image: Chermaine Lee/DW Advertisement A United States Marine was arrested on suspicion of murder in Okinawa, Japan , police said Sunday, prompting an official protest from the Japanese government. The 20-year-old lance corporal is suspected of robbing and murdering a 39-year-old woman in a hotel in Naha, the capital of Japan's most southernmost prefecture. Japanese public broadcaster NHK reported that CCTV footage showed a foreign man entering a hotel room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings. Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and who voluntarily accompanied them to a local police station where he was arrested. The suspect reportedly denies the charges. What have Japanese officials said? "The occurrence of ​such an extremely brutal and vicious incident is extremely regrettable," said Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi ​in a statement as Tokyo registered an official protest with Washington. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has lodged an official complaint with Washington Image: Yudai Kato/Jiji Press/picture alliance "The government of Japan strongly protests to the US side and strongly seeks maximum cooperation with the investigation," she continued, also calling for "stricter discipline among US military personnel" and "thorough measures" to prevent a recurrence. According to the local Asahi Shimbum newspaper, the brother of the victim said: "We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened. My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter." The US Marine Corps confirmed that a serviceman assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force and based at Marine Corps Air Station at Futenma, Okinawa, was in Japanese custody. "The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the ⁠highest ​standards of behavior," it said in a statement. The US Ambassador to Japan, George Glass, said he had spoken with Japan's Foreign Ministry and Okinawa's governor, offering "sincere condolences and pledging full cooperation as the investigation continues." Pacifist Japan is rearming — this is why To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video How many US Marines are in Okinawa — and why? The United States has around 54,000 military personnel, including 18,000 Marines, stationed in Japan. Most are based in Okinawa , which the US captured during the Second World War and held until 1972 . Located only 100 kilometers (60 miles) from Taiwan at the closest point, Okinawa is considered by both Tokyo and Washington to be key in deterring potential aggression from China in the region. But the US presence regularly stirs resentment among local residents over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and the conduct of personnel, with crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run incidents and drunk-driving accidents. "Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen," said Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi. According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, around 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested in Okinawa since 1972. In 2024, that number hit 80, the highest in 20 years. Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a US Marine to seven years in prison after finding him guilty of choking and attempting to rape a young woman. In 2017, a former US Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
